title: Advances in LLM Architecture
oneLiner: Today's LLMs are still Transformers, but with four upgrades: steadier normalisation, rotating position signals, gated activations, and many 'expert' networks of which only a few run per word.

what.html:
The basic Transformer block (attention plus a small feed-forward network) has been refined piece by piece. Normalisation moved to the front of each layer and got cheaper. Position is now encoded by rotating vectors. The feed-forward network uses a gate that decides what passes. And Mixture of Experts gives a model many feed-forward networks but uses only two or so for each word.

Everyday versionSame car, better parts: smoother suspension (normalisation), a better speedometer (position), a smarter fuel valve (gating), and a garage of specialist engines where only the right two start for each trip (experts).

why.html:
• These pieces appear in nearly every modern model description.
  • They explain why deep models train stably and handle long text.
  • Mixture of Experts explains how some models are huge yet fast to run, and still memory-hungry.

how.title: Normalise first
how.html: Normalising the input of each layer (pre-norm) instead of its output keeps a clean shortcut from the first layer to the last, so very deep models train without blowing up.

how.title: A cheaper normaliser
how.html: RMSNorm just divides by the typical size of the numbers and skips subtracting the average: [2, −1, 3, 0] becomes [1.07, −0.53, 1.60, 0]. Cheaper, and just as good.

how.title: Position by rotation
how.html: RoPE turns each word's vectors by an angle set by its position. Two words the same distance apart always end up at the same angle, so attention sees "how far apart" rather than "where".

how.title: Smooth curves and gates
how.html: GELU and SiLU are smooth versions of ReLU. A gated unit multiplies two signals: one says how much to let through, the other carries the content.

how.title: SwiGLU
how.html: A SiLU gate inside the feed-forward layer. With the width trimmed to keep the size equal, it learns better than the plain version, so most new models use it.

how.title: Many experts, few at a time
how.html: A small router sends each word to the best 2 of, say, 8 expert networks. Only 25% of the expert weights do any work for that word.

how.title: The catch
how.html: Every expert still has to be stored in memory, and the router must be nudged to spread work evenly, or a few experts get overloaded while others sit idle.

demo.html: Match each description to the architecture advance it belongs to.

example.html:
Active vs total. 8 experts, each with 134 million parameters, top-2 routing: the layer stores about 1.07 billion parameters but each word uses 268 million, a quarter of them.

Supplementary Stretching a model's context window often works by slowing RoPE's rotation speeds, so positions far beyond the training length still land on familiar angles.

misunderstandings: MoE models are cheap to store.
All experts must be in memory.
RoPE adds a position vector to the input.
RMSNorm is a rough approximation that hurts quality.
Width is cut to keep the size equal.
takeaways: Pre-norm keeps a clean residual path; RMSNorm is cheaper.
RoPE rotates q and k so scores depend on relative distance.
GELU/SiLU are smooth; gates (GLU) control what passes.
SwiGLU beats a plain MLP at equal size.
MoE: top-k of E experts (2/8 = 25% active); memory and balancing costs.
thirty: Modern LLMs refine the Transformer block. Pre-norm (h + F(Norm h)) keeps a clean identity path and trains stably at depth, unlike post-norm (Norm(h + F h)). RMSNorm divides by the root-mean-square and skips mean subtraction ([2, −1, 3, 0] → [1.07, −0.53, 1.60, 0]), cheaper with no quality loss. RoPE rotates each q/k dimension pair by position × θᵢ so q·k depends only on relative distance, generalising to longer context. GELU and SiLU are smooth ReLUs; GLUs multiply a gate by content; SwiGLU (SiLU gate, width cut to ~8d/3 for equal parameters) beats GELU MLPs. Mixture of Experts routes each token to the top-k of E experts (2/8 = 25% active), giving big capacity at modest per-token compute, but all experts must be stored and routing needs load balancing (auxiliary loss, capacity limits).
